title: Simple-hyperplane criterion for representations of a perfect Lie algebra
statement: Let $k$ be a field and let $L$ be a $k$-Lie algebra [def-wf-lie-algebra] that is perfect: $L$ is the $k$-linear span of its brackets $[x,y]$. A finite-dimensional representation is a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space $M$ [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace] with a linear map $\rho:L\to\operatorname{End}_k(M)$ satisfying $\rho([x,y])=\rho(x)\rho(y)-\rho(y)\rho(x)$. A subspace is invariant if it is preserved by every $\rho(x)$, and a representation is simple if it is nonzero and its only invariant subspaces are $0$ and itself. Suppose that for every finite-dimensional representation $M$ of $L$ and every simple invariant subspace $W\subseteq M$ with $\dim_k(M/W)=1$, there exists an invariant subspace $D\subseteq M$ with $M=W\oplus D$. Then every invariant subspace $U$ of every finite-dimensional representation $V$ of $L$ has an invariant complement $C$, with $V=U\oplus C$. Here a direct sum means that each vector has a unique expression as a sum of vectors from the two indicated subspaces. No finite-dimensionality of $L$, characteristic-zero hypothesis, or algebraic closure of $k$ is assumed.

source.place: Section 22c, Lemma 22.40, printed pp.476-477: agent adaptation of its simple-hyperplane criterion and Hom-space proof to Lie modules for a perfect Lie algebra over any field; this Lie-module formulation is not the algebraic-group statement of the printed lemma.

proof.text: Fix $L,k$ and the simple-hyperplane splitting hypothesis. Subspaces, quotients and inverse images of invariant subspaces carry the restricted or quotient action: $x\cdot(v+A)=x\cdot v+A$, well-defined because $A$ is invariant, and the representation identity descends. We use finite dimensions throughout. A quotient is spanned by the images of a finite basis; a subspace has a basis of at most the ambient dimension (successively choose independent vectors until they span). Thus these constructions stay finite-dimensional. On a one-dimensional invariant space $T$, choose $t\ne0$ and write $x\cdot t=\chi(x)t$. Linearity makes $\chi:L\to k$ linear, and the representation identity gives $\chi([x,y])=\chi(x)\chi(y)-\chi(y)\chi(x)=0$. Perfectness gives $\chi=0$, so every invariant line is trivial.

source.place: Lemma 22.40, printed pp.476-477; agent adaptation from group actions with no characters to Lie actions of a perfect Lie algebra.

proof.text:
Prove by strong induction on $n=\dim M$ that every invariant hyperplane $W\subset M$ has an invariant complement. For $n=0$ there is no hyperplane. If $W=0$, take $M$; if $W$ is simple, use the hypothesis. Otherwise choose a proper invariant subspace $A\subsetneq W$ of largest dimension. Since $W$ is nonzero and not simple, a proper nonzero invariant subspace exists, so $A
e0$. Such a largest dimension exists among $0,\ldots,\dim W-1$. Every invariant subspace of $W/A$ has invariant inverse image in $W$; maximality of $\dim A$ implies $W/A$ is simple. Choose $m
otin W$. The map $(W/A)\oplus k	o M/A$, $(w+A,a)\mapsto w+am+A$, is a vector-space isomorphism. Hence $W/A$ is an invariant hyperplane of $M/A$. Since $A
e0$, the dimension formula gives $\dim(M/A)<n$. The induction hypothesis therefore gives an invariant line $\overline D\subset M/A$ with $M/A=(W/A)\oplus\overline D$.

source.place: Lemma 22.40, printed pp.476-477; agent adaptation from group actions with no characters to Lie actions of a perfect Lie algebra.

proof.text: Let $P$ be the inverse image of $\overline D$ in $M$. It is invariant, $P\cap W=A$, and $M=W+P$: both claims follow by taking images in the displayed quotient direct sum. The quotient map gives $P/A\cong\overline D$, so $A$ is a hyperplane in $P$. The dimension formula yields $\dim P=\dim A+1<\dim W+1=\dim M$, since $A\subsetneq W$. Apply the induction hypothesis again, now to $(P,A)$, obtaining $P=A\oplus D$ with $D$ invariant. Then $M=W+D$ and $W\cap D\subseteq A\cap D=0$. This completes the induction. The second induction application is essential; an arbitrary vector-space splitting of $P/A$ would not give an invariant $D$.

source.place: Lemma 22.40, printed pp.476-477; agent adaptation from group actions with no characters to Lie actions of a perfect Lie algebra.

proof.text: For the desired pair $(V,U)$, take $C=V$ if $U=0$ and $C=0$ if $U=V$. Otherwise put $H=\operatorname{Hom}_k(V,U)$. The cited Lie-Hom action gives $(x\cdot f)(v)=x\cdot f(v)-f(x\cdot v)$. The space $H$ is finite-dimensional: relative to finite bases of $V$ and $U$, the finitely many maps sending one basis vector to one basis vector and the others to zero span $H$. Thus every subspace of $H$ below is a finite-dimensional representation when invariant.

source.place: Lemma 22.40, printed pp.476-477; agent adaptation from group actions with no characters to Lie actions of a perfect Lie algebra.

proof.text: Put $E=\{f\in H:f|_U=a\operatorname{id}_U\text{ for some }a\in k\}$ and $K=\{f\in H:f|_U=0\}$. They are linear subspaces. For $f|_U=a\operatorname{id}_U$ and $u\in U$, invariance of $U$ gives $(x\cdot f)(u)=a(x\cdot u)-a(x\cdot u)=0$. Hence $x\cdot E\subseteq K$ and $x\cdot K\subseteq K$, so both are invariant. Because $U\ne0$, the scalar $a$ is unique, defining a linear map $s:E\to k$ with kernel $K$. To see it is onto, use a vector-space complement $V=U\oplus B$ from the cited complement lemma; the projection $p(u+b)=u$ lies in $E$ and satisfies $s(p)=1$. More explicitly $f=s(f)p+(f-s(f)p)$ decomposes $E=kp\oplus K$, so $K$ is a hyperplane in $E$.

source.place: Lemma 22.40, printed pp.476-477; agent adaptation from group actions with no characters to Lie actions of a perfect Lie algebra.

proof.text: Apply the hyperplane splitting proved in steps 2-3 to $K\subset E$: obtain an invariant line $D$ with $E=K\oplus D$. Choose $0\ne f\in D$. Step 1 makes the action on $D$ trivial, so for all $x,v$, $0=(x\cdot f)(v)=x\cdot f(v)-f(x\cdot v)$; thus $f:V\to U$ is equivariant. Since $D\cap K=0$, its scalar $a=s(f)$ is nonzero. Set $q=a^{-1}f$. Then $q|_U=\operatorname{id}_U$ and $q$ is equivariant. The subspace $C=\ker q$ is invariant, since $q(x\cdot c)=x\cdot q(c)=0$. For each $v\in V$, $v=q(v)+(v-q(v))$ has its first term in $U$ and its second in $C$. If $u\in U\cap C$, then $u=q(u)=0$. The expression is therefore unique and $V=U\oplus C$, as required.
